title: India to Supply 654 MW Power Daily to Flood-Ravaged Nepal
excerpt: New Delhi's Ministry of Power cleared 18-hour daily electricity exports to the Nepal Electricity Authority through December 31, after August floods erased about a tenth of Nepal's hydropower capacity.
body:
• India's Ministry of Power approved exports of up to 654 MW of electricity to Nepal for 18 hours a day, from midnight to 6 pm, effective September 13 through December 31, 2026.
  • Up to 600 MW will move through the Muzaffarpur–Dhalkebar 400 kV line and 54 MW through the Tanakpur–Mahendranagar 132 kV line, to the Nepal Electricity Authority.
  • The August 26 floods, set off by an ice-rock avalanche near the Nepal–Tibet border, killed nearly 1,400 people and damaged or swept away more than a dozen hydropower plants — about a tenth of Nepal's generation capacity.
  • India has flown eight relief missions carrying over 130 tonnes of supplies to Kathmandu; Nepal says it needs $5 billion for initial rebuilding.

What New Delhi approved

India's Ministry of Power announced on September 14 that it had cleared exports of up to 654 megawatts of electricity to Nepal for 18 hours a day, from midnight to 6 pm, starting September 13 and running through December 31, 2026, according to the Times of India.

The bulk of the supply — up to 600 MW — will flow through the Muzaffarpur–Dhalkebar 400 kV double-circuit line, with a further 54 MW on the Tanakpur–Mahendranagar 132 kV single-circuit line. The Nepal Electricity Authority is the designated buyer.

The ministry added that the quantum of power exported from January 2027 would be reviewed in December 2026, making this a winter bridge rather than an open-ended commitment.

"The approval will help Nepal meet its power requirements during this difficult period and further strengthen the close and longstanding energy cooperation between India and Nepal."

— Ministry of Power, Government of India

Context and background

The floods struck on August 26, triggered by an ice-rock avalanche near the Nepal–Tibet border, and tore through northern and central Nepal — including Bagmati province, the country's main hydropower-producing region.

According to Nepal's National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority, the death toll had reached 1,385 as of September 11, with 5,130 people still missing. More than a dozen hydropower plants were swept away or badly damaged, and about 900 power station workers are among the missing, Reuters reported — a loss of skilled staff on top of lost hardware.

Reuters reported the deluge wiped out roughly a tenth of Nepal's generation capacity, cutting domestic generation by about 550 MW. Hydropower supplies almost all of Nepal's electricity, so the damage struck at the heart of the power system just before the dry season.

Impact and analysis

Until last month, the power flow mostly ran the other way. Nepal exported its monsoon hydropower surplus to India, and hydropower had become a fast-growing source of export revenue. That has now reversed: Nepal has halted exports, which are down nearly 400 MW from peak levels of about 1,000 MW, and will buy from India to cover domestic shortfalls.

The Nepal Electricity Authority will procure the additional electricity through the Day-Ahead Market and Real-Time Market segments of Indian power exchanges during non-solar hours — a market mechanism aimed at Nepal's evening and early-morning demand. Nepal normally begins seeking Indian imports around October as river flows fall; this year's approval arrived a month early.

The wider bill is far larger than a power contract. Nepali officials said last week they would ask wealthier countries and global agencies to contribute to the $5 billion needed for initial rebuilding, arguing the disaster shows how climate change is hitting poor countries that did little to cause it. Nepal has asked China to rebuild the Syaphrubesi–Rasuwagadhi road — Infrastructure Development Minister Sunil Lamsal told The Kathmandu Post that Beijing has given a verbal commitment, though no written agreement is signed. The United States approved $1 million for Nepal Police's forensic capacity, taking Washington's post-flood support past $5 million.

Diaspora angle

Nepal and India share an open border, and millions of Nepalis live and work in India. For those families, this is not abstract energy policy — it is whether hospitals, schools and homes keep power through the winter. India's parallel relief effort — eight special flights carrying more than 130 tonnes of supplies, with 54 personnel deployed — is the first-responder role Nepali diaspora communities, from India to the Gulf and the US, have come to expect from New Delhi when a neighbour is hit.

What's next

The December review will set the export quantum from January 2027 — the depth of winter, when Nepal's rivers run low and domestic generation dips further. Whether the 18-hour window or the 654 MW ceiling changes will signal how confident both sides are in the repair timeline.

The longer clock is the rebuild of the plants swept away in Bagmati province. Until those are restored, India's grid — and its power exchanges — remain Nepal's backstop, and a former exporter stays a buyer.
nri_angle: For South Asian diaspora communities — especially Nepalis living and working in India — India's rapid power supply and relief response demonstrates New Delhi acting as first responder when an open-border neighbour is hit.
author: Diaspora Desk
